sources.citation: Ahland, Michael Bryan. 2012. A grammar of Northern Mao (Màwés Aas'è). PhD dissertation, University of Oregon, xxxiv+742 pp. (PDF 775 pp.)
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Nothing. Ch. II 'Contrastive phonology' (pp. 52-94, incl. 2.4 syllable structure, 2.5 tonal melodies) and Ch. III 'Tone' (pp. 95-192) describe a three-level tone system (H, M, L; M with two underlying sources; downstep; construct-noun melodies; tone as stem-category marker). Full-text grep for stress/accent/prominence/intensity returns only non-phonological uses ('distress', 'stress that', a remark about Amharic pronoun stress p. ~400, and 'increase in volume and a higher register' for pragmatic emphasis on a demonstrative, ch. 6). No word-stress or accent statement anywhere.

sources.citation: Ahland, Michael. 2009. Aspects of Northern Mao (Bambassi-Diddesa) phonology. Linguistic Discovery 7(1): 1-42. doi:10.1349/PS1.1537-0852.A.332
sources.note: Nothing. Sections: 2 consonants, 3 phonemic vowels/length, 4 syllable, 5 tonal melodies (p. 22ff.), 6 conclusions. Section 5 opens 'Northern Mao, like other Omotic languages, exhibits contrastive tone' and establishes three tone levels with F0 measurements; no mention of stress, accent or prominence in the whole article (grep of PDF text and HTML text: zero hits).
